title: Decision: the catch-up participation-window bound is a SHOULD, not a MUST
description:
docs/design/mimi-catchup.md §8, §8.1.

An earlier draft of the note made the participation-window bound a MUST
and said a loose bound was "a worse hole than the one being fixed".

DECIDED by Mark, 2026-11-22: SHOULD, not MUST. "Getting it wrong is just
an efficiency problem not an interop problem."

He is right, and the MUST framing was wrong:

- A provider is not a member of the MLS group. It holds no group keys
  and never decrypts application content; only its users' clients do.
  Fanout from sequences when it had nobody in the room is ciphertext it
  cannot read. A loose bound wastes the hub's bandwidth and the
  follower's storage; it does not hand over message content.
- A loose bound is also undetectable. The requester cannot tell whether
  what it got was bounded correctly, and a correct hub and a sloppy one
  are indistinguishable to every other implementation. A MUST whose
  violation no peer can observe and no test can catch buys conformance
  language and nothing else.

Recorded in §8.2 so the SHOULD is not read as "does not matter": a loose
bound still leaks that fanouts occurred, when, and how large they were,
plus whatever handshakes carry outside the ciphertext -- an MLS
PublicMessage handshake is authenticated, not encrypted, so membership
changes from periods the requester was absent for would be readable.
mimid follows the SHOULD. It is just not a thing to fail a peer over.

The test this establishes, applied to the note's other keywords: §5.1
and §6's "a hub MUST answer an out-of-window request distinctly" stays
a MUST, because a follower behaves differently depending on the answer
(it surfaces a gap instead of showing a silent hole), so a violation is
observable on the wire and testable by the requester. That is
correctness, not bandwidth.

Carried into mimid-1wgh.37.104.2 and .3.
